children: National Australia Bank (NAB) shares are on track to record its worst one-day decline since February 2025, down 6.2% to $38.58 at noon after bad debt charges for FY26 nearly doubled year-on-year, and well-above analyst expectations.

The bank also suffered after-tax one-off charges of $949 million for the year, driven by an accounting policy shift to write down and immediately expense software development costs, which dragged cash earnings down 13.4% to $6.14 billion.
The one-day decline has now flipped NAB into negative year-to-date territory, down 5.2%, despite being up as much as 18% for the year in late February.
FY26 at a glance
All comparisons are against Macquarie’s pre-result estimates.
Cash earnings down 13.4% to $6.14bn vs $6.36bn ests (3.4% miss)
Excluding one-offs, flat at $7.09bn
Underlying profit down 5.4% to $10.38bn vs $10.47bn ests (0.9% miss)
Credit impairment charge up 86% to $1.55bn vs $1.36bn ests (13.5% above)
Net interest margin up 6 bps to 1.80% vs 1.80% ests (in line)
Diluted cash earnings per share of 198.8 cents vs 207 cents ests (4.0% miss)
Final dividend of 85 cents, fully franked, taking the full year to 170 cents vs 170 cents ests (in line)
CET1 ratio of 11.87%, or 12.07% pro forma
Bad debts drive a sizeable miss

The impairment charge came in $184 million or 13.5% above Macquarie forecast, though underlying profit missed by less than 1%. Of the $1.55 billion charge, $1.08 billion related to individual customers, mostly business borrowers in the corporate and business banking books.

NAB also added $403 million to forward-looking provisions, citing: "We have strengthened provisioning to reflect a more challenging environment of slowing growth, declining house prices, higher interest rates and inflationary pressures."
Bad debts ran at 0.19% of loans, up from 0.11% and the highest of the past five years. Home loan arrears also rose, though fast loan growth kept the overall default ratio down 4 bps at 1.22%.
NAB’s economic outlook
NAB’s economists expect the economy to keep slowing, pointing to the 125 bps of RBA rate hikes since February 2026 to tackle inflationary pressures.
Its forecasts:
Real GDP growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 1.0% in 2027, then some improvement in 2028
Unemployment rising gradually to about 5.5% by early 2028
The RBA cash rate on hold at 4.85% “for a while”
The housing market correction adding downside risk to growth
On the consumer, Australian home lending balances grew 3.8%. NAB said it “maintained a disciplined approach to growth as the market became more challenging over 2H26."

The bottom line: NAB is still growing loans and deposits, and the all-important net interest margin and dividend came in line with expectations. But with the RBA cash rate at an 18-year high, a sixfold jump in home borrowers in negative equity and rising stress among small business owners servicing home loans from business income, it’s perhaps no surprise NAB booked a jump in impairments and set aside more for the road ahead.

NAB’s selloff comes on a day the S&P/ASX 200 is up almost 2%, rallying after the Democratic sweep at the US midterm elections. The other major banks would likely be trading higher if not for NAB’s result.

While NAB’s economists expect slower growth and higher unemployment, investors are piling into consumer-facing and yield-sensitive parts of the market like retailers and REITs. The market, at least, seems to think there are better days ahead.
Credit impairment charges rose 86% to $1.55bn, 13.5% above Macquarie’s forecast. Most came from business borrowers, with a further $403m added to forward-looking provisions.
Cash earnings fell 13.4% to $6.14bn after $949m in one-off charges, driven by a software accounting change. Excluding one-offs, earnings were flat at $7.09bn.
Net interest margin rose 6 bps to 1.80% and the 170-cent full-year dividend matched forecasts. NAB’s economists expect unemployment to reach about 5.5% by early 2028.

title: NAB FY26 result: Shares head for worst day since February 2025 as bad debts nearly double
